# Guideline 4 - Play for the scene, not just yourself The best rounds happen when players give each other something to play with. Your character does not need to be the hero of every story; sometimes the best thing you can do is make someone else's moment better.
- Give people something to react to. Talk to the crew around you, share rumours, have opinions, and let others into your character's day. - Say "yes, and" where you can. Build on what other players start instead of shutting it down, even if your character disagrees. - Let losing be interesting. Getting arrested, outsmarted or hurt can be a great scene when you play it out rather than rushing past it. - As an antagonist, you are one of the storytellers of the round. Give your targets and security something to discover, chase and react to.
## Examples Good: - A chef who notices a scientist looking stressed and asks about it, starting a conversation that runs the whole shift. - A prisoner who argues their case, bargains with the warden and tries to talk their way out. - A traitor who leaves clues and builds tension, so the crew has a mystery to solve.
Not what we are looking for: - Ignoring everyone who talks to you so you can get on with your own goals. - Shrugging off an arrest or an interrogation with one-word answers until it is over. - As an antagonist, finishing your objectives so quietly and quickly that nobody else ever gets to take part.
